title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 1)
text: This will be the first blog post in a two-part introduction to multigrid. For those of you who are new to numerical linear algebra, you are certainly welcome to read as I have designed these posts for those who are unfamiliar with numerical methods entirely! However, you may have a greater appreciation for what is being discussed if you are at least familiar with Jacobi/Gauss-Seidel iteration. The only “hard” prerequisites are an understanding of linear algebra (specifically eigenvalue problems and bases) and calculus.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 1)
text:
Motivation
While multigrid is considered a numerical linear algebra technique, it was originally developed for finding numerical solutions of PDEs. So, we will use a boundary value problem (BVP) to help us understand how multigrid works, why it’s so helpful, and how it can be generalized.
Suppose we want to find the numerical solution to the following BVP:
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
-\Delta u(\mathbf{x}) + a(\mathbf{x})u(\mathbf{x}) = 0,\qquad &\text{in }\Omega\\
u(\mathbf{x}) = g(\mathbf{x}),\qquad &\text{on }\partial\Omega,
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where \Omega denotes the domain and \partial\Omega denotes its boundary. The specifics of the PDE aren’t too important, but it is noteworthy that this is an elliptic PDE.

Definition 1 (Elliptic PDE) Suppose we have the following linear second-order PDE for an unknown function of two variables u(x,y):
Au_{xx} + 2Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + Du_{x} + Eu_y + Fu + G = 0
where the coefficients A,B,\ldots,G may be constants or functions of x and y. This PDE is called elliptic at a point (x,y) if

B(x,y)^2-A(x,y)C(x,y)<0.

It is elliptic on \Omega if this condition holds at every point in \Omega.

As it turns out, we don’t call this an elliptic PDE for no reason. As a fun side exercise, maybe try to figure out why this family of PDEs may be called “elliptic” :). However, I don’t want to get too far off track here. The reason I want to distinguish this family of PDEs is because this was the family of PDEs for which multigrid was originally designed.
This all sounds well and good… but how does this relate to numerical linear algebra? Well, for PDEs such as this, we can easily discretize them into a linear system: \begin{equation}
\mathbf{Au} = \mathbf{f}.
\end{equation}
For the purposes of this post, I will just tell you that we can discretize PDEs using finite difference methods. I will perhaps explain in a future post how and why these help with discretizing PDEs, but, for now, I will just give you the central difference method for second derivatives: 
f''(x_i)\approx \frac{f(x_{i+1}) - 2f(x_i) + f(x_{i-1})}{h^2},

where x_i is the point we want to evaluate the derivative at, and h is the size of the steps between x points. So how does this help us represent a BVP as a linear system? Let’s look at an example.

Example (1D Poisson)

\begin{split}
-u''(x) = f(x),\qquad 0<x<1\\
u(0) = u(1) = 0.
\end{split}

Let’s say we want to find an approximation v to u. We can represent the approximation v as a vector \mathbf{v} where the i-th element is v(x_i), and we do the same for f by representing it as a vector \mathbf{f}. Then, using the central difference method, we can express the BVP as:

\frac{1}{h^2}\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & & & & \\
-1 & 2 & -1& & & \\
& -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\
  &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
  &  & & \ddots & \ddots &  -1\\
&  & &  & -1 &  2\\
\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{f},

For later discussions, we will define:
\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & & & & \\
-1 & 2 & -1& & & \\
& -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\
  &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
  &  & & \ddots & \ddots &  -1\\
&  & &  & -1 &  2\\
\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{A}_h = \frac{1}{h^2}\mathbf{T}.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 1)
text:
Approximating Solutions
In numerical linear algebra, we have two key quantities for characterizing the accuracy of an approximate solution \mathbf{v} to the true solution \mathbf{u}.

Definition 2 (Error) The error is defined as \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.


Definition 3 (Residual) The residual is defined as \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{f} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}.

As it turns out, the error and residual are directly related: \mathbf{Ae} =\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}) = \underbrace{\mathbf{Au}}_{=\mathbf{f} \text{ by (2)}} - \mathbf{Av} = \mathbf{f} - \mathbf{Av} = \mathbf{r}.
But how can we actually obtain an approximation \mathbf{v}? A common approach is to use an iterative method. Much time in a numerical linear algebra class is spent discussing these, and so we will not go into too much detail here. However, I do want to discuss one iterative scheme, the weighted Jacobi method (WJM).

Definition 4 (Weighted Jacobi Method) For solving the linear system given in (2), we can utilize the following iterative update called the weighted Jacobi method to obtain an approximation to the solution \mathbf{u}:
\mathbf{u}^k = ((1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega\mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{F}))\mathbf{u}^{k-1} + \omega\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{f},
where \omega \in [0,1], \mathbf{D} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{A}), and -\mathbf{E} and -\mathbf{F} are the strict lower and strict upper parts of \mathbf{A} respectively.

Similarly, the exact solution applied to the WJM update gives us:
\mathbf{u} = ((1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega\mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{F}))\mathbf{u} + \omega\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{f},
So, if we take the difference of the true solution and our update (which is our approximation), we can write the error at step k as:
\mathbf{e}^k = ((1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega\mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{F}))\mathbf{e}^{k-1}\equiv \mathbf{G}\mathbf{e}^{k-1}.
Alternatively, if we have initial error \mathbf{e}^0, after k iterations, we can write this as:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{e}^k = \mathbf{G}^k\mathbf{e}^0.
\end{equation}
To emphasize, in the abstract, \mathbf{G} can represent the error-propagation matrix of any stationary linear iterative method, I am simply choosing it to represent WJM for the purposes of later discussions. If the structure of the update doesn’t seem intuitive to you do not worry, for the purposes of this post’s story, just try to have a grasp on what each component of the update scheme represents.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 1)
text:
Smoothing Effects
Now, suppose \{\lambda_j, \boldsymbol{\varphi}_j\}_{j=1}^m are eigenpairs of \mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}. Let’s also assume that \mathbf{G} is diagonalizable. Then, we know that the eigenvectors of \mathbf{G} form a basis for \mathbb{R}^m. Then we can represent any vector in \mathbb{R}^m in terms of a linear combination of the eigenvectors of \mathbf{G}. Since \mathbf{e}^0\in\mathbb{R}^m, for some coefficients \alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}, we have:
\mathbf{e}^0 = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j\boldsymbol{\varphi}_j.
Plugging this into (3), we have:
\mathbf{e}^k = \mathbf{G}^k \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j\boldsymbol{\varphi}_j.
The eigenproblem \mathbf{G}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_j = \lambda_j \boldsymbol{\varphi}_j can be used to show, by induction, that \mathbf{G}^k\boldsymbol{\varphi}_j = \lambda_j^k \boldsymbol{\varphi}_j. Thus, we have:
\mathbf{e}^k = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j (\lambda_j)^k \boldsymbol{\varphi}_j.
So how do the eigenvalues affect how quickly different components are damped? If |\lambda_j|\ll 1, the j-th component is damped very quickly. If |\lambda_j|\approx 1, the component is reduced very slowly. If |\lambda_j|>1, the component instead grows.
At this abstract level, we should refer to these as rapidly damped and slowly damped components. Whether they correspond to high- or low-frequency modes depends on the spatial behavior of the associated eigenvectors. We will see this relationship explicitly for the one-dimensional Poisson problem.

Example (Return to 1D Poisson Equation)
We will return to the discretization we discussed earlier. We can represent the eigenvalue problem of this discretization as:
\mathbf{T}\mathbf{v} = \mu\mathbf{v}.

(Optional) Derivation of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors for 1D Poisson
If you do not want to see the derivation of the eigenvectors/eigenvalues of this BC, you can skip this section. Though, I recommend you read through it as it provides insight into the trigonometric nature of the spectrum of this problem.
For the i-th component, we have:
-v_{i-1} + 2v_i - v_{i+1} = \mu v_i.
Using the methods of constant coefficients, we can guess that v_i = r^i for some r, then we have:
-r^{i-1} + 2r^i -r^{i+1} = \mu r^i
\Rightarrow r^2 - (2-\mu)r + 1 = 0
So, we have guesses r_1 and r_2. Then, for a particular v_\ell, we have:
v_\ell = \alpha r_1^\ell + \beta r_2^\ell.
Next, we can use the boundary conditions. Plugging these both in leads to solving a system of equations (which I will leave as an exercise to the reader), but the end result gives us:
\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^n = 1.
We divide [0,1] into n subintervals, so h=\frac{1}{n}. Because two boundary values are prescribed the discrete solution has n-1 unknown components. This means that the ratio r_1/r_2 is an n-th root of unity:
\frac{r_1}{r_2} = e^{\frac{2\pi ij}{n}},\quad j =1,2,\cdots, n-1.
Again, since r_1,r_2 are both roots of the original quadratic equation, we know that:
(r-r_1)(r-r_2) = 0
\Rightarrow r^2 - (r_1 + r_2)r + r_1r_2 =0.
Thus, going back to our original expression for the quadratic equation, means that we must have:
\begin{split}
r_1+r_2 = 2-\mu\\
r_1r_2 =1\quad \Rightarrow r_1 = \frac{1}{r_2}.
\end{split}
Because r_1/r_2 has unit magnitude and r_1r_2=1, both roots have unit magnitude. Thus, up to swapping the roots, we may write

r_1=e^{\mathrm{i}\theta},
\qquad
r_2=e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}.

The boundary condition gives

\left(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^n
=
e^{2\mathrm{i}n\theta}
=
1.

Therefore,

\theta=\frac{\pi j}{n},
\qquad
j=1,2,\ldots,n-1,

and hence

r_1=e^{\pi\mathrm{i}j/n},
\qquad
r_2=e^{-\pi\mathrm{i}j/n}.

Then, by the first equation, we have:
\mu_j = 2 - (r_1+r_2) = 2 - \left(e^{\frac{\pi ij}{n}} +  e^{-\frac{\pi ij}{n}}\right).
Now, recall that we can define cosine in terms of exponentials \cos(x) = \frac{e^{ix} + e^{-ix}}{2}. Thus, we can further simplify our j-th eigenvalue:
\mu_j = 2 - 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi j}{n}\right),
= 2\left(1 - \cos\left(\frac{\pi j}{2n} + \frac{\pi j}{2n} \right)\right).
Using the double angle formula, we get:
= 2\left(1 - \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi j}{2n}\right) + \sin^2\left(\frac{\pi j}{2n}\right)\right).
Using \cos^2x + \sin^2x = 1:
= 4\sin^2 \frac{\pi j}{2n},\quad j=1,2,\cdots, n-1,
hence, we have the eigenvalues. For the j-th eigenvector, we recall that:
v_\ell^{(j)} = -r_1^\ell + r_2^\ell = -e^{\frac{\pi ij\ell}{n}} + e^{-\frac{\pi ij\ell}{n}} = -2i\sin\left(\frac{\pi j \ell}{n} \right).
Finally, since eigenvectors/eigenfunctions can be scaled by any non-zero constant, we can obtain the corresponding grid mode, including its prescribed boundary values:
\begin{bmatrix}
v_0^{(j)}\\
v_1^{(j)}\\
\vdots\\
v_{n-1}^{(j)}\\
v_n^{(j)}
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\sin\frac{\pi j(0)}{n}\\
\sin\frac{\pi j(1)}{n}\\
\vdots\\
\sin\frac{\pi j(n-1)}{n}\\
\sin\frac{\pi j(n)}{n}
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
0\\
\sin\frac{\pi j}{n}\\
\vdots\\
\sin\frac{\pi j(n-1)}{n}\\
0
\end{bmatrix}.
Since the boundary values are prescribed, we write the eigenvector in n-1 dimensions as:
\mathbf{v}^{(j)} = \begin{bmatrix}
\sin\frac{\pi j}{n}\\
\sin\frac{2\pi j}{n}\\
\vdots\\
\sin\frac{\pi j(n-1)}{n}
\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}
PHEW!


Behavior of Iteration on Different Frequencies
We briefly mentioned low vs. high-frequency components in the previous section. However, I would like now to provide a more specific definition for this specific problem. Recall the eigenvalues for this problem are given as:
\mu_j = 4\sin^2 \frac{\pi j}{2n},\quad j=1,2,\cdots, n-1.
We can see that the eigenvalues of \mu_j increase with j. However, the frequency of mode j is determined by the behavior of its eigenvector. As we can see in the figure below, a smaller value for j will vary much less across the grid than a higher one. Hence, we call the former a low-frequency mode and the latter a high-frequency mode.








Figure 1: Low- and high-frequency eigenmodes for the one-dimensional Poisson problem with n=9.







Analysis of Weighted Jacobi Method on Different Frequencies
So we can visualize the high-frequency and low-frequency modes of the discretization matrix, but how can we see how these different modes converge for the weighted Jacobi iteration. For this discretization,

\mathbf{D}_h
=
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{A}_h)
=
\frac{2}{h^2}\mathbf{I}.
 First, we can rewrite the weighted Jacobi iteration matrix as the following:
\mathbf{G} = (1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{E}+\mathbf{F})
=(1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega \mathbf{D}_h^{-1}(\mathbf{D}_h-\mathbf{A}_h)
=(1-\omega)\mathbf{I} + \omega\mathbf{I} - \omega\mathbf{D_h}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_h
=\mathbf{I} -\omega\mathbf{D}_h^{-1}\mathbf{A}_h
=\mathbf{I} - \omega \left(\frac{h^2}{2}\mathbf{I}\right)\left(\frac{1}{h^2}\mathbf{T}\right)
=\mathbf{I} - \frac{\omega}{2}\mathbf{T}.
Now, from our derivation of the eigenvalues of \mathbf{T}, we can easily translate those to the eigenvalues of \mathbf{G}, which are 1 - \frac{\omega}{2}\left(4\sin^2 \frac{\pi j}{2n}\right) =
1 - 2\omega \sin^2\frac{\pi j}{2n} for j=1,2,\cdots, n-1.
Let us consider the case where \omega=\frac{2}{3}, then, the eigenvalues become:
\gamma_j = 1 - \frac{4}{3}\sin^2 \frac{\pi j}{2n}.
For j=n-1,

\begin{aligned}
\gamma_{n-1}
&=
1-\frac{4}{3}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi(n-1)}{2n}\right)\\
&=
1-\frac{4}{3}
\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right)\\
&=
-\frac{1}{3}
+\frac{4}{3}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right)\\
&=
-\frac{1}{3}
+\frac{\pi^2h^2}{3}
+\mathcal{O}(h^4).
\end{aligned}

Thus, |\gamma_{n-1}|\approx 1/3, so this oscillatory mode is rapidly damped. Its sign alternates between iterations because \gamma_{n-1}<0 for n\geq 4.
For j=1,

\begin{aligned}
\gamma_1
&=
1-\frac{4}{3}
\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi h}{2}\right)\\
&=
1-\frac{\pi^2h^2}{3}
+\mathcal{O}(h^4)\\
&\approx 1.
\end{aligned}

Therefore, the smooth mode is reduced very slowly.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 1)
text:
Takeaway
In this post, we gave a primer on the motivation for multigrid methods. For weighted Jacobi applied to this discretized elliptic problem, the high-frequency error components are rapidly damped, while the low-frequency components decay slowly. This motivates a method for handling these low-frequency modes, which we will discuss in the next post. Sorry for the cliffhanger :).

title: What Is a PDE?
text: If your physics knowledge comes mostly from brilliant communicators like Neil deGrasse Tyson or Brian Cox, you aren’t alone. However, while pop science is fantastic for sparking curiosity, it rarely gives you the tools to look under the hood yourself. To really understand the universe—and eventually, to teach machine learning models how to simulate it—we have to speak its native language: Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). I know that term can be a massive mental barrier. If you’ve had bad experiences with math in the past, PDEs can sound incredibly intimidating. My goal in this first post is to completely demystify them. If you have a basic grasp of limits and derivatives, you have everything you need to follow along.

title: What Is a PDE?
text:
Partial Derivatives
Let f(x,y) be a function of two variables. We can take a derivative with respect to one variable, while the other is held constant. These are the partial derivatives, or partials, of f.

\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x+h,y) - f(x,y)}{h},
 
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \lim_{k\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x,y+k)-f(x,y)}{k}.

In practical terms, if f(x,y) describes a surface, then f_x measures how the surface changes as we move in the x-direction while keeping y fixed. Similarly, f_y measures the change in the y-direction while x is fixed.

Example
Suppose we have the function:
f(x,y) = x^2 + 3xy.
Differentiating with respect to x and holding y constant gives us:
f_x(x,y) = 2x+3y,
while differentiating with respect to y and holding x constant gives us:
f_y(x,y) = 3x.

title: What Is a PDE?
text:
Definition of a PDE
A PDE is a relationship between an unknown function u(x,y,\cdots) of at least two variables, its partials, and functions of the independent variables. The order of a PDE is the highest derivative appearing.
More formally, a PDE is an equation of the form:
F(x_1,x_2,\cdots, x_n, u, u_{x_1}, u_{x_2},\cdots, u_{x_1 x_2},\cdots) = 0,
where x_1,\cdots x_n are the independent variables, u is the unknown function (also called the dependent variable) that depends on these variables, and u_{x_i}, u_{x_{i} x_{j}} represent the partial derivatives of u with respect to the independent variables. Note that we do not stop at order two in the general case. Higher-order PDEs occur as well, although first- and second-order equations are the most common examples in an introductory course.

Examples

Transport Equation

\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0,\qquad \text{Order = 1}

Laplace’s Equation

\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} = 0,\qquad \text{Order = 2}

Heat Equation

\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \kappa\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2},\qquad \text{Order = 2}
Note that for the heat equation, although it contains only a first derivative with respect to time, it is second order because u_{xx} is a second derivative.

title: What Is a PDE?
section: What Does it Mean to Solve a PDE?
text:
What Does it Mean to Solve a PDE?
For now, we will use the “classical” notion of a solution. A sufficiently differentiable function u solves a PDE on a domain D if substituting u and its partial derivatives into the equation makes the equation true at every point in D. If the problem also includes initial or boundary conditions, then u must satisfy those conditions as well.

Example
u(x,t) = e^{-t}\sin(2x)
Does u solve 4u_t = u_{xx}? Let’s find out!
u_t = -e^{-t}\sin(2x)\quad\Rightarrow\quad 4u_t = -4e^{-t}\sin(2x),
u_x = 2e^{-t}\cos(2x)\quad\Rightarrow\quad u_{xx} = -4e^{-t}\sin(2x).
So, we can verify that this particular u solves the given PDE! (If you look closely, you can verify that this is a variation of the heat equation with diffusivity \kappa = \frac{1}{4}). Well, that wasn’t so bad… is this really all physicists do? Well, as it turns out, checking if a given function is a solution to a PDE is much more straightforward than actually finding solutions. And “the solution” is perhaps an improper phrase to use. A PDE by itself often has an infinite number of solutions. Initial and boundary conditions help determine which solution describes the particular situation we care about. Even after initial and boundary conditions are supplied, many PDE problems do not have a useful closed-form solution. In those cases, numerical methods allow us to approximate the solution on a computer.
Everything I just said will make more sense in future blog posts, but it should be well-established that the process of finding solutions to PDEs is not as straightforward as finding solutions to algebraic equations you may have dealt with in the past. This is not to say it is more difficult, but it certainly requires a different approach.
Some unanswered questions go deeper than finding a convenient closed-form formula. In certain cases, fundamental questions about the existence and regularity of solutions remain unresolved. A famous example is the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes system. The associated Millennium Prize Problem asks, roughly speaking, whether smooth solutions arising from suitable smooth initial data always remain smooth for all time, or whether they can develop singularities (Fefferman 2006). As of July 2026, the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved, with 1 million US dollars allocated to its solution (Clay Mathematics Institute, n.d.).

title: What Is a PDE?
section: Optional Deep Dive: Derivation of a 1D Wave Equation
text:
Optional Deep Dive: Derivation of a 1D Wave Equation
To cap off this first post, I would like to do a derivation relating to physics so that you can see how valuable PDEs are for modelling the world around us. To fully follow along with this derivation, I recommend the reader also have some knowledge of antiderivatives and integration as well as Newton’s second law.
Suppose an elastic string of length \ell has both ends tied down and is subject to transverse waves. Let u(x,t) denote the vertical displacement of the string at horizontal position x and time t. Assume that the string has uniform linear mass density \rho, measured in kg/m, and that its motion is purely transverse. Because the endpoints are fixed, we have:
u(0,t) = u(\ell, t) = 0.
Further, we assume that its slope is small in magnitude (|u_x|\ll 1), and damping and external forces are neglected.



Illustration of a string tied down at two ends x=0 and x = \ell


Now, we can zoom in and pick two distinct points on the string x_0 and x_1. At the endpoints of this segment, the tangent to the string makes angles \theta_0 and \theta_1 with the horizontal. The corresponding tension magnitudes are T(x_0) and T(x_1) respectively:



Zoomed in perspective of the string analyzed between two distinct points x_0 and x_1.


Now, we have to balance the forces. Since there is no horizontal acceleration (the string only vibrates) the forces will add up to zero.
T(x_1)\cos(\theta_1) - T(x_0)\cos(\theta_0) = 0.
However, there is a vertical acceleration. So, we can obtain the total vertical force using Newton’s second law F = ma, where the vertical acceleration of the string is u_{tt}. Between points x_0 and x_1, we can take the integral of mass density times acceleration to give us the net vertical force:
T(x_1)\sin(\theta_1) - T(x_0)\sin(\theta_0) = \int_{x_0}^{x_1}\rho u_{tt}dx.



Right triangle relating the slope of the string to its tangent angle.


Now, using the right triangle that is formed by the angle and vertical change (demonstrated above) we can observe that:
\sin(\theta) = \frac{u_x}{\sqrt{1+u_x^2}},\qquad \cos(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+u_x^2}}.
Under the small-slope assumption, |u_x| \ll 1, we approximate the \sin and \cos values as:
\sin(\theta) \approx u_x,\qquad \cos(\theta) \approx 1.
So, under the small-slope approximation, the horizontal force balance becomes:
T(x_1) -T(x_0)\approx 0.
Therefore, to leading order, we treat the tension magnitude as constant along the string and denote it by T. This is handy, because we can now substitute this into our vertical force balance equation:
T(u_x(x_1,t) - u_x(x_0,t)) = \rho\int_{x_0}^{x_1} u_{tt}(x,t)dx.
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we know that:
u_x(x_1,t) - u_x(x_0,t) = \int_{x_0}^{x_1}u_{xx}(x,t)dx.
Thus, we obtain:
T\int_{x_0}^{x_1}u_{xx}(x,t)dx = \rho\int_{x_0}^{x_1}u_{tt}(x,t)dx.
Because this equality holds for every interval [x_0,x_1], and because the integrands are continuous, the integrands must be equal:
Tu_{xx} = \rho u_{tt}.
And, if we define c:= \sqrt{\frac{T}{\rho}} (where c denotes the speed at which waves propagate along the string), we obtain the one-dimensional wave equation in its familiar form:
u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}.
Voilà! Of course, this is just a 1D string and physics can get quite a bit more complicated than this, but the premise of modelling physical phenomena with the help of PDEs is a consistent theme throughout many areas of physics.
Note: This is just a reminder that we did not solve the 1D wave equation, we simply derived the PDE that defines the dynamics. As it turns out, solving this PDE analytically requires a bit more mathematics, which will potentially be discussed in future blog posts.

title: What Is a PDE?
text:
Takeaway
A PDE is not merely an equation containing unusual derivative symbols. It is a local rule describing how a quantity changes with respect to multiple independent variables—often space and time. Together with appropriate initial and/or boundary conditions, that rule can become a mathematical model of a physical system.
We have not yet solved the wave equation—or any other PDE in a systematic way. That is where the next parts of this series will lead: first toward analytical methods, then numerical approximation, and eventually toward the ways scientific machine learning can learn from or work alongside these equations.
All figures are my own.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text: In Part 1, we saw that weighted Jacobi quickly damps oscillatory error but reduces smooth error very slowly. In this post, we will explore how coarse grids help address the error that relaxation leaves behind.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Recap and Motivation

Let us recall the 1D Poisson problem we saw in Part 1:
\begin{split}
-u''(x)  &= f(x),\quad 0<x<1\\
u(0) &= u(1) = 0
\end{split}
Take n equal intervals, with h=1/n and interior nodes x_\ell=\ell h for \ell=1,\ldots,n-1. The central difference method gives the discrete system: 
\frac{1}{h^2}\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & & & & \\
-1 & 2 & -1& & & \\
& -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\
  &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
  &  & & \ddots & \ddots &  -1\\
&  & &  & -1 &  2\\
\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{f},

with:
\mathbf{T} = \begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & & & & \\
-1 & 2 & -1& & & \\
& -1 & 2 & -1 & & \\
  &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
  &  & & \ddots & \ddots &  -1\\
&  & &  & -1 &  2\\
\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{A}_h = \frac{1}{h^2}\mathbf{T}.
Let \mathbf{u}_h^* be the exact solution of this discrete system and \mathbf{v}_h^k its current iterative approximation. Define the algebraic error by \mathbf{e}^k=\mathbf{u}_h^*-\mathbf{v}_h^k; this is distinct from the error caused by discretizing the PDE.
Also recall that, for a consistent linear stationary iterative method, we can represent the error after k iterations as: 
\mathbf{e}^k = \mathbf{G}^k\mathbf{e}^0

where \mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} is the error-propagation matrix and m=n-1. If \mathbf{G} is diagonalizable, we can expand \mathbf{e}^0=\sum_{j=1}^m\alpha_j\boldsymbol{\varphi}_j in its eigenvector basis and write:

\mathbf{e}^k = \sum_{j=1}^m \alpha_j (\lambda_j)^k \mathbf{\varphi}_j.

This assumption holds for weighted Jacobi on our 1-D Poisson problem: its error-propagation matrix is symmetric. It does not hold for every stationary iteration.
The question that remains open from last time is: how do we remove the components of the error associated with eigenvalues for which |\lambda_j|\approx 1—that is, the parts of the error that decay slowly?

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Using Smoothing Effects
To address the low-frequency components of the error, we can use a “coarser” grid. A wave that is smooth relative to the fine-grid spacing varies more rapidly relative to the coarse-grid spacing. No new frequency information is created: we sample the same wave at fewer points. Here, coarsening means increasing the mesh spacing and reducing the number of interior unknowns.
But this sounds counterintuitive at first. Intuitively, you might assume that a coarser grid provides less usable detail—like watching a movie on a 1970s box TV instead of a modern IMAX screen. However, consider a broad, gentle slope spanning thousands of fine-grid pixels. To a local smoother inspecting adjacent pixels on the IMAX screen, that slope looks nearly flat, so the smoother barely adjusts it.
When we represent that same smooth error on a coarse grid, the spatial distance between grid points increases. Its physical shape does not change, but its variation from one grid point to the next becomes more pronounced. Some modes that relaxation handles poorly on the fine grid can therefore be reduced more effectively on a coarser grid. The smoothest modes may still need further coarsening. This is how I got myself to understand this nuanced idea, but an actual example may make it clearer.
Let us again consider the matrix \mathbf{T}. First, we will take n = 8, giving us the following frequencies/modes:
With the convention from Part 1, n=8 means eight grid intervals and seven interior unknowns. The eigenmodes are v_\ell^{(j)}=\sin(\pi j\ell/8) for j=1,\ldots,7.






Figure 1: Eigenmodes for j=1,\ldots,7 with n=8. The dots show the grid values; the smooth sine curves are visual guides.



Now consider n=4: the grid spacing is h=1/4, and there are three interior unknowns. The corresponding eigenmodes are v_\ell^{(j)}=\sin(\pi j\ell/4) for j=1,2,3.






Figure 2: Eigenmodes for j=1,2,3 with n=4. The dots show the grid values; the smooth sine curves are visual guides.



Of course, the plots look the same, but our evaluation points become fewer and farther apart. With this new discretization, j=1 remains a smooth mode, while modes j=2 and j=3 now become higher-frequency modes. But… why?

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Why a Coarser Grid Helps
Let us consider the j=2 case from the previous example. The fine grid has spacing h=1/8 and n=8 intervals; the coarse grid has spacing H=2h=1/4 and N=n/2=4 intervals. On the fine grid, this mode has components

v_{h,\ell}^{(2)}=\sin\left(\frac{2\pi\ell}{8}\right).

Its dimensionless angular frequency is \theta_h=\pi j/n=\pi/4, so j/n=1/4 is its frequency relative to the grid’s Nyquist limit \theta=\pi. This measures oscillation relative to the mesh spacing, not a fraction of the grid’s eigenmodes.
To isolate the sampling effect, retain every second fine-grid value (a transfer called injection). Coarse index \ell corresponds to fine index 2\ell, giving

v_{H,\ell}^{(2)}=v_{h,2\ell}^{(2)}
=\sin\left(\frac{2\pi(2\ell)}{8}\right)
=\sin\left(\frac{2\pi\ell}{4}\right),\qquad \ell=0,\ldots,N.

The normalized frequency is now j/N=1/2, at the start of the coarse grid’s high-frequency band. The physical wave has not changed; its angular frequency per grid step has doubled.
For weighted Jacobi with \omega=2/3, the amplification factor for mode j on a grid with n intervals is

\gamma_j^{(n)}=1-\frac{4}{3}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi j}{2n}\right).

Thus \gamma_2^{(8)}\approx0.805, whereas \gamma_2^{(4)}=1/3. One sweep reduces this mode’s amplitude much more on the coarse grid. More generally, |\gamma_j^{(n)}|\leq1/3 for n/2\leq j\leq n-1. This smoothing statement is specific to the weighted-Jacobi choice above; ordinary Jacobi does not uniformly damp the high-frequency modes.
In the actual multigrid algorithm, we restrict the residual and solve a coarse error equation. Injection here illustrates the frequency change; the weighted restriction introduced below also changes the mode amplitudes.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
section: What Happens to Fine High Frequencies?
text:
What Happens to Fine High Frequencies?
What if we consider j=5? This mode is already high-frequency on the fine grid. Can its coarse samples distinguish it from every lower-frequency mode? (Try to answer this yourself.)
Answer in 3…2…1…
NO! The coarse grid has only three independent interior modes. The fine-grid j=5 mode becomes indistinguishable, up to a sign, from the coarse-grid j=3 mode. For N=4, its samples are

v_{h,2\ell}^{(5)}=\sin\left(\frac{5\pi\ell}{N}\right).

Using the sine difference identity,

\begin{aligned}
\sin\left(\frac{(2N-5)\pi\ell}{N}\right)
&=\sin\left(2\pi\ell-\frac{5\pi\ell}{N}\right)\\
&=\sin(2\pi\ell)\cos\left(\frac{5\pi\ell}{N}\right)
-\cos(2\pi\ell)\sin\left(\frac{5\pi\ell}{N}\right)\\
&=-\sin\left(\frac{5\pi\ell}{N}\right).
\end{aligned}

Hence v_{h,2\ell}^{(5)}=-v_{H,\ell}^{(3)}. This is aliasing: different fine-grid modes give the same coarse samples up to a scalar factor.
More generally, for N<j\leq n-1 and n=2N,

v_{h,2\ell}^{(j)}=-v_{H,\ell}^{(n-j)}.

The boundary case j=N=n/2 is different: all its coarse samples are \sin(\pi\ell)=0. The coarse grid therefore cannot represent every fine-grid error component independently. Notice also that an aliased mode need not be low-frequency on the coarse grid: in our example, j=3 is its highest mode.
This motivates the main idea behind multigrid methods:

Use a few weighted-Jacobi sweeps on \Omega^h to reduce high-frequency error before transferring information to a coarser grid.
Restrict the residual to \Omega^{2h} and approximately solve the coarse error equation. Prolongate that correction to reduce error that was smooth on the fine grid.
Apply the same idea recursively on \Omega^{4h},\Omega^{8h},\ldots, solving directly on the coarsest grid. Return through the levels with corrections and post-smoothing, then repeat cycles until the desired tolerance is reached. A finite number of sweeps does not generally eliminate all error exactly.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
The Four Corners of Multigrid






NoteA note on the reference



The framework below draws on Olson (2015), particularly the discussion of smoothing, grid-transfer operators, and Galerkin coarse-grid correction. The author’s manuscript is freely available. I use different notation here: n counts grid intervals, and h_0 denotes the coarsest mesh spacing.



Hierarchy of Grids
Let us assume that we have a hierarchy of grids. We start from the finest grid with a mesh size of h. Then, the grid on the next level will have a mesh size of 2h, the one after that 4h, etc. For the coarsest grid, we denote it by h_0 = 2^{L-1}h (where L is the number of levels we have). The physical grid at the finest level will be denoted as \Omega^h and \Omega^{h_0} is the grid at the coarsest level.
We choose nested grids so that each coarse node is a fine node. For the examples here, n is a power of two and the coarsest grid has two intervals, leaving one interior unknown.






Figure 3: A four-level hierarchy on [0,1] with h=1/16 and h_0=8h=1/2. Each notch marks a grid point. Each coarser grid retains every second point of the preceding grid, doubling the mesh spacing.





Interpolation/Prolongation
We have spoken much about these different grid discretizations, but we have yet to discuss how we actually TRANSFER between these discretizations. First, we will discuss the operator that brings us from a coarse grid to the finer grid at the next level up. This is called the interpolation/prolongation operator. It maps values defined on the coarse grid to values on the fine grid. For n=2N intervals and homogeneous Dirichlet boundary values, its action on the interior vectors is:
\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h: \mathbb{R}^{N-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{n-1}.
Then, for quantities \mathbf{x}_h and \mathbf{x}_{2h} defined on grids \Omega^h and \Omega^{2h} respectively, we can define the explicit prolongation as:
\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h\mathbf{x}_{2h} = \mathbf{x}_h
Designing prolongation matrices is a major research subfield of multigrid methods (to be discussed in later posts). For now, though, let us consider a simple example: linear interpolation.
At the even points on the fine grid, we copy the coarse values: v_{h,2\ell}=v_{2h,\ell} for \ell=0,\ldots,N. At the odd points, we interpolate between adjacent coarse values. These are estimates of the missing values, not a recovery of arbitrary fine-grid data. Linear interpolation gives:
v_{h,2\ell+1} = \frac{1}{2}(v_{2h,\ell} + v_{2h,\ell+1}),\qquad \ell=0,\ldots,N-1.
With v_{2h,0}=v_{2h,N}=0, the matrix acting on the interior values for N=4 and n=8 is:
\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h\mathbf{v}_{2h} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
1 & & \\
2 & & \\
1 & 1 & \\
  & 2 & \\
  & 1 & 1\\
  & & 2\\
  & & 1
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{v}_{2h,1}\\
\mathbf{v}_{2h,2}\\
\mathbf{v}_{2h,3}
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{v}_{h,1}\\
\mathbf{v}_{h,2}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{v}_{h,7}
\end{bmatrix}






Figure 4: Linear prolongation from four to eight intervals, with zero boundary values. New fine-grid values lie on the same piecewise-linear interpolant.





Restriction
The operator that transfers fine-grid values to the coarse grid is called restriction. For the same interior vector spaces, it has the mapping:
\mathbf{R}_h^{2h}: \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N-1}.
More specifically, we can write the restriction as:
\mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{x}_h =\mathbf{x}_{2h}
As with prolongation, there are many restriction operators. Here we choose transpose restriction, \mathbf{R}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}, which is commonly paired with the Galerkin coarse operator \mathbf{A}_{2h}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{P}. Restriction alone is not the Galerkin projection. Using our prolongation matrix gives:
\mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{v}_h = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 1 &   &   &  & \\
  &   & 1 & 2 & 1 &  & \\
  &   &   &   & 1 & 2 & 1
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{v}_{h,1}\\
\mathbf{v}_{h,2}\\
\vdots\\
\mathbf{v}_{h,7}
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{v}_{2h,1}\\
\mathbf{v}_{2h,2}\\
\mathbf{v}_{2h,3}
\end{bmatrix}






Figure 5: Restriction from eight to four intervals using the matrix \mathbf{R}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} above. Each interior coarse value is a weighted sum with weights (1/2,1,1/2); the boundary values remain zero. Both panels use the same vertical scale.



The weights here are (1/2,1,1/2), a weighted sum. The common 1-D full-weighting choice instead uses \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{FW}}=\tfrac12\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}, with weights (1/4,1/2,1/4). We use transpose restriction throughout this post, including the code. With either convention, form both the coarse matrix \mathbf{A}_{2h}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{P} and the coarse right-hand side \mathbf{r}_{2h}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{r}_h consistently. Multiplying both by the same nonzero scalar leaves the exact coarse correction unchanged.


Iterative Methods and the Two-Grid Scheme
We have already discussed iterative methods a bit, but some additional context is needed to better understand how they fit into the entire “multigrid” story. On the finest grid we solve for the solution; on coarser grids we approximately solve error equations. You may or may not know, from numerical linear algebra, that one way we can find crude approximations to the solutions of linear systems is through iterative methods (as was discussed a bit in Part 1). Let’s say, for example, we had a simple two-grid scheme. That is, we have a single fine grid and a single coarse grid. Then, the algorithm would proceed as follows:
With our error convention, \mathbf{e}_h=\mathbf{u}_h^*-\mathbf{v}_h and \mathbf{r}_h=\mathbf{f}_h-\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h satisfy \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{e}_h=\mathbf{r}_h. This explains why we solve for a coarse error correction and add its prolongation to the current approximation.

Iterate on the fine-level problem \mathbf{A}_h \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{f}_h to reach \mathbf{v}_h via a few iterations of an iterative method like weighted Jacobi or Gauss-Seidel.
Restrict the residual \mathbf{r}_h = \mathbf{f}_h - \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h to the coarse grid by applying a designated restriction operator:
\mathbf{r}_{2h} = \mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{r}_h
Solve the coarse approximation to the error equation, with homogeneous boundary values:
\mathbf{A}_{2h}\mathbf{e}_{2h} = \mathbf{r}_{2h}
Prolongate the coarse correction and update the fine approximation:
\mathbf{v}_h\leftarrow\mathbf{v}_h+\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h\mathbf{e}_{2h}.
Apply a few more smoothing sweeps to \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h=\mathbf{f}_h, starting from the corrected \mathbf{v}_h.

Note: You may be wondering: how do we find \mathbf{A}_{2h}? It turns out, we RAP! Not in the Kendrick Lamar way, but the “let’s restrict and prolongate our fine-level discretization” way. More specifically, we have:
\mathbf{A}_{2h} = \mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{A}_h \mathbf{P}_{2h}^h.
For our fine-grid finite-difference matrix and linear interpolation, the choice \mathbf{R}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} gives \mathbf{A}_{2h}=2\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{2h}, where \widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{2h} is obtained by directly discretizing on spacing 2h. Full weighting would give \widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{2h} itself. This scaling does not change weighted-Jacobi’s error-propagation matrix, since its diagonal scales by the same factor.
Here \mathbf{A}_h is symmetric positive definite and \mathbf{P} has full column rank, so \mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{P} is invertible. For \mathbf{R}=\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}} and an exact coarse solve, the fine-space operator \mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{P})^{-1}\mathbf{P}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{A}_h is the Galerkin projection onto the range of \mathbf{P}, orthogonal in the \mathbf{A}_h inner product. The error after correction is (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})\mathbf{e}_h. This precisely removes errors in that coarse space, but not arbitrary fine-grid errors.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Multigrid Scheme
A convergent two-grid method can reach the desired algebraic accuracy, but its coarse solve may still be expensive on a large problem. Multigrid addresses that cost by approximately solving the coarse error equation with another two-grid scheme, and repeating this recursively until the coarsest problem is small. Hence multigrid (finally)! One way to organize this recursion is a V-cycle: visit each coarser grid once, then return through the finer grids, correcting and smoothing along the way.







NoteAlgorithm: one multigrid V-cycle



Input: current mesh spacing h, right-hand side \mathbf{f}_h, and initial approximation \mathbf{v}_h.
Setup: choose smoothing counts \nu_1,\nu_2 and construct the grid hierarchy, transfer operators, and coarse matrices \mathbf{A}_{2h}=\mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h in advance. Write this routine as \operatorname{VCycle}(h,\mathbf{f}_h,\mathbf{v}_h).

Coarsest grid: if h=h_0, solve \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h=\mathbf{f}_h directly and return \mathbf{v}_h.
Pre-smooth: apply \nu_1 relaxation sweeps to \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h=\mathbf{f}_h, starting from the current \mathbf{v}_h.
Compute and restrict the residual:

\mathbf{r}_h=\mathbf{f}_h-\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h,
\qquad
\mathbf{r}_{2h}=\mathbf{R}_h^{2h}\mathbf{r}_h.

Recurse on the coarse error equation, starting from zero:

\mathbf{e}_{2h}\leftarrow\operatorname{VCycle}(2h,\mathbf{r}_{2h},\mathbf{0}).

Prolongate and correct:

\mathbf{v}_h\leftarrow\mathbf{v}_h+\mathbf{P}_{2h}^h\mathbf{e}_{2h}.

Post-smooth: apply \nu_2 relaxation sweeps to \mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h=\mathbf{f}_h, starting from the corrected approximation.
Return the updated \mathbf{v}_h.



To solve the original problem, repeat V-cycles on the finest grid until \|\mathbf{f}_h-\mathbf{A}_h\mathbf{v}_h\|_2\leq\max(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\|\mathbf{f}_h\|_2) or a chosen maximum number of cycles is reached. The coarse calls solve for an error correction, so they use homogeneous boundary conditions for this Dirichlet problem.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Watching a V-Cycle
The animation follows one cycle through six levels, from h=1/64 to h_0=1/2. On the way down, we smooth and restrict the residual. On the way up, we prolongate the error correction and smooth again. The highlighted node marks the current stage; the notches show its grid. This is an illustration of the traversal, not a plot of error magnitude.






Figure 6: One V-cycle: descend through the grids, solve on the coarsest grid, and return with corrections.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Computational Experiment
For a concrete version of our Poisson problem, take

-u''(x)=\pi^2\sin(\pi x),\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0,

whose exact solution is u(x)=\sin(\pi x). The code below starts from zero on a grid with n=64 intervals and applies V-cycles until the relative residual is below 10^{-10}. Each cycle uses two weighted-Jacobi sweeps before and after the coarse correction, with \omega=2/3.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def hierarchy(n):
    """Interior Dirichlet matrices and linear transfer operators."""
    if n < 2 or n & (n - 1):
        raise ValueError("n must be a power of two, at least 2")
    A = n**2 * (2 * np.eye(n - 1)
                 - np.eye(n - 1, k=1) - np.eye(n - 1, k=-1))
    matrices, transfers = [A], []
    while n > 2:
        P = np.zeros((n - 1, n // 2 - 1))
        for col in range(P.shape[1]):
            P[2 * col:2 * col + 3, col] = [0.5, 1, 0.5]
        R = P.T
        matrices.append(R @ matrices[-1] @ P)
        transfers.append(P)
        n //= 2
    return matrices, transfers


def smooth(A, b, v, sweeps=2, omega=2/3):
    for _ in range(sweeps):
        v = v + omega * (b - A @ v) / np.diag(A)
    return v


def v_cycle(matrices, transfers, level, b, v):
    A = matrices[level]
    if level == len(matrices) - 1:
        return np.linalg.solve(A, b)
    v = smooth(A, b, v)
    P = transfers[level]
    coarse_rhs = P.T @ (b - A @ v)
    coarse_error = v_cycle(matrices, transfers, level + 1,
                           coarse_rhs, np.zeros_like(coarse_rhs))
    v = v + P @ coarse_error
    return smooth(A, b, v)


n = 64
x = np.linspace(0, 1, n + 1)
b = np.pi**2 * np.sin(np.pi * x[1:-1])
matrices, transfers = hierarchy(n)
A = matrices[0]
v = np.zeros(n - 1)
relative_residuals = [np.linalg.norm(b - A @ v) / np.linalg.norm(b)]

for cycle in range(50):
    v = v_cycle(matrices, transfers, 0, b, v)
    relative_residuals.append(np.linalg.norm(b - A @ v) / np.linalg.norm(b))
    if relative_residuals[-1] < 1e-10:
        break
else:
    raise RuntimeError("V-cycles did not reach the residual tolerance")

# Check the iterative result against a direct solve of the same discrete system.
np.testing.assert_allclose(v, np.linalg.solve(A, b), rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
print(f"V-cycles: {len(relative_residuals) - 1}")
print(f"Final relative residual: {relative_residuals[-1]:.2e}")
print(f"Maximum error against sin(pi*x): {np.max(np.abs(v - np.sin(np.pi*x[1:-1]))):.2e}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.4))
xx = np.linspace(0, 1, 500)
axes[0].plot(xx, np.sin(np.pi * xx), color="#8a8a8a", label="Exact solution")
axes[0].plot(x, np.r_[0, v, 0], ".", color="#235789", label="Multigrid")
axes[0].set(xlabel="x", ylabel="u(x)")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)
axes[1].semilogy(range(len(relative_residuals)), relative_residuals,
                 "o-", color="#235789", markersize=4)
axes[1].set(xlabel="Completed V-cycles", ylabel="Relative residual")
for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.set_facecolor("none")
fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
plt.rcParams["savefig.transparent"] = True
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

V-cycles: 10
Final relative residual: 4.26e-11
Maximum error against sin(pi*x): 2.01e-04








Figure 7: The multigrid approximation and exact solution, alongside the relative residual after each V-cycle.





The residual measures how well we solve the discrete system. Its convergence does not remove the finite-difference discretization error, which is why the error against \sin(\pi x) remains larger. This compact example uses dense matrices for readability; a large multigrid solver would use sparse matrices or stencil operations.

title: Demystifying Multigrid (Part 2)
text:
Closing Thoughts
Congrats! Now you can brag to your friends and family that you know what all the kids are talking about: multigrid methods. Still, this short series was just a primer on this subfield of numerical analysis, and there is much left unsaid about more “sophisticated” versions of this idea. However, they all rest on the same principles we discussed in these two posts. In future posts, I hope to delve deeper into multigrid and even talk about “neural” multigrid methods (one of my primary research interests).
